summary: Marina sits on the former Fort Ord military base, meaning a significant portion of the city's 9.8 square miles is still transitioning from decommissioned army land into housing, retail, and open space — a process decades in the making that gives the landscape a patchwork quality rare for coastal California. That military legacy also means direct access to thousands of acres of trails, dunes, and oak woodlands in the Fort Ord National Monument, right at the city's eastern edge, while the western side faces Monterey Bay with flat, sandy terrain and cool marine air that keeps the annual average high around 65°F year-round — no scorching summers, no real winters, just persistent mildness and occasional fog. The home price-to-income ratio sits around 8.6×, steep but notably below neighboring Monterey and Pacific Grove, which helps explain why newer subdivisions keep sprouting on former base land. Cal State Monterey Bay anchors the southern end, making the city partly a college-adjacent economy alongside healthcare and public-sector jobs clustered along the peninsula, though many commuters drive Highway 1 south to Monterey or north toward Santa Cruz. The retail and dining scene remains thin relative to those neighbors — strip-center oriented rather than walkable-downtown oriented — and evening activity is quiet. Marina is essentially a housing-growth story unfolding on repurposed federal land, with genuine coastal access and moderate climate as the draw, and an identity still catching up to its construction pace.
